title: Hillary and Tenzing Reach the Summit Together
text:
The 1953 British Everest expedition, led by John Hunt, was a large team effort. Hundreds of porters and a strong group of Sherpas carried supplies up through the Khumbu Icefall and the Western Cwm, while climbers took turns breaking trail and stocking camps higher on the mountain. On 26 May the first assault pair, Tom Bourdillon and Charles Evans, reached the South Summit but had to turn back, exhausted and with failing oxygen.

Three days later Edmund Hillary, a beekeeper from New Zealand, and Tenzing Norgay, the experienced Sherpa climber, left their tiny tent at about 27,900 feet. They passed the South Summit, climbed a steep rock and snow step on the ridge, and at about 11:30 in the morning of 29 May stood on the highest point on Earth. Hillary photographed Tenzing holding up his ice axe hung with flags. There is no summit photograph of Hillary.

Back in the world, the press and politicians kept asking one question: who stepped onto the top first? It became a nationalist quarrel in India and Nepal. For a time the two men simply said they had arrived together.

In his autobiography, Tiger of the Snows (1955), Tenzing settled it himself: Hillary had been slightly ahead, and Tenzing came up just after him. He added that it did not matter, because they had climbed as a team, roped together, and the summit belonged to both of them and to everyone who had carried them there.
lesson: Shared achievements rarely survive a fight over credit. Agree early that the win belongs to the whole team, and it stays a win.
people: Edmund Hillary, Tenzing Norgay, John Hunt
source: John Hunt, The Ascent of Everest (1953); Tenzing Norgay with James Ramsey Ullman, Tiger of the Snows (1955)
